player.text: The water is rising in the tunnel and the crates are still on the platform. Mara has to choose between the cargo and helping Dell, who is trapped under a beam.

data.text:
The water is black and cold, licking at the base of the crates. I can hear the groan of the beam above Dell, a sound like a ship’s hull splitting under a heavy swell. My hand hovers over the ledger, the ink still wet, but the numbers are blurring.

I look at the cargo. Three crates of salted cod, worth more than my last three years of wages. I look at Dell, his face pale in the dim light, one arm pinned beneath the timber.

"The manifest says it all," I say. My voice is steady, but my fingers are trembling. "If we lose the cod, the debt stays. If we lose you, the debt stays, but I lose the one who remembers why I started."

I step away from the ledger. The water rises another inch, soaking the hem of my coat. I reach out and take Dell’s hand, pulling him gently toward the dry side of the platform.

"Leave it," I say. "The cod can wait. You can’t."

I let go of his hand and turn back to the crates. The water is already lapping at the first one. I watch it for a second, then look at Kell, who is standing by the tunnel’s exit, waiting.

"Move the last two," I tell Kell. "Leave the first. It’s already soaked through."

I walk back to Dell, my eyes on the water, my heart on the choice.

The timber presses against my ribs, a solid, unyielding weight that keeps my breath short. Mara’s hand is warm against my palm, a small, dry thing in the cold. I do not pull away. I watch her turn back to the crates, her shoulders squared against the dark.

"Kell," I say, my voice rough from the pain. "Do not let the water take the ledger."

I am already moving before the word leaves his mouth. The last two crates are heavy, but the wet brick is slick under my boots, and I do not stop to count the cost of the muscle I burn. I haul the first one up onto the dry platform, setting it down with a thud that shakes the floor. The water is already over the top of the third crate, the one I was told to leave. I do not look at it. I look at the ledger, which is still in Mara’s hand, still dry, still the only thing in this tunnel that has not been drowned or broken.

"Here," I say, turning to face her. I hold the ledger out, my hands steady despite the strain in my shoulders. "The numbers are safe. The debt is not."

Mara takes the ledger from Kell’s hands. The paper is dry, but the weight of it has changed. It is no longer just numbers. It is a promise made to men who are already dead, or men who will be, if the water keeps rising.

"Kell," I say, my voice low. "The first crate is gone. The debt is still here."

I look at Dell. He is breathing, but each breath is a struggle. The beam above him creaks, a sound that feels personal, like it knows his name. I cannot lift it. I cannot carry him. I can only hold the ledger, and I can only choose.

I look at the water, then at the crates, then at Dell. The choice is not between the cargo and the man. It is between the debt and the life.

"Dell," I say. "Can you stand?"

He does not answer. He is too busy breathing.

I turn to Kell. "We leave the ledger. We take the man. If the cod is worth more than his life, then I have been counting wrong all along."

I hand the ledger back to Kell. "Hold it. Keep it dry. I am going to get him out."

I wait. The water laps at the first crate, closer now. I do not blink. I am not counting the cost of the muscle I burn, or the time we lose. I am only waiting for his answer, and for the ledger to stay dry.

I look at Kell. He is holding the ledger against his chest like a shield, his knuckles white. The question hangs in the damp air, heavy and wet. I try to answer, but the beam shifts, a low groan that vibrates through my ribs.

"I can stand," I say.

The words are a lie, or maybe a hope. I brace my good arm against the wet brick, my fingers slipping on the moss. The pain is a white spike behind my eyes. I look at Mara. She is watching me, her face tight, the ledger gone from her hands.

"Then move," I say. "Before the water decides for us."

"Move," she says to him, not looking up. "Now. While the wood still holds."

She takes a step toward the light at the tunnel’s end, her grip on Dell tightening. The water rushes in to fill the space the beam left behind.

The wood drops behind us with a crack that sounds like a bone breaking. Dust plumes in the dim light, settling on my shoulder. I am not standing. I am being carried, a dead weight against Mara’s side, my good arm slung over her shoulder. The bad arm hangs loose, fingers brushing the wet brick as we move.

The beam’s shadow is gone. In its place, the water rushes in, filling the gap it left behind. It is faster than I expected, a dark, hungry thing that swallows the space where the timber lay.

I look at Kell. He is still there, the ledger pressed to his chest, his knuckles white. He is not moving. He is not looking at the water. He is looking at the first crate, the one that is now half-submerged, its salt-stained wood darkening as it takes on the tide.

Mara does not stop. The light at the tunnel’s mouth is a thin, white slit, cutting through the dark. The water is at my knees now, heavy and cold, pulling at my legs with every step. Dell is a dead weight against my side, his breath shallow and quick, a sound that is almost like a whisper.

I feel Kell’s eyes on my back. I do not turn. I can feel the ledger in his coat, a dry, hard thing against his chest. He is holding the debt. I am holding the man.

"Dell," I say, my voice low, meant only for him. "Do not close your eyes. If you close your eyes, I will have to carry you all the way to the shore, and I will not do it gently."

He does not answer. His head lolls against my shoulder. I tighten my grip on his arm, pulling him up, forcing him to stand on his own two feet, even if they are trembling. The water rushes around us, filling the space where the platform used to be.

"Kell," I call out, not looking back. "Keep the numbers dry. The debt will wait for us on the other side."

The water is at my waist now, cold and heavy, pressing against the wool of my coat. I do not let go of the ledger. I tuck it tighter, pressing the dry paper into the hollow of my chest, feeling the pulse of my own heart hammering against the debt.

I watch Mara move. She is not running. She is wading, her boots sinking into the silt, her face set in a line of hard, quiet decision. She has made her choice. The man is in her arms. The cargo is in the water.

I look at the first crate, the one I left behind. It is gone now, swallowed by the dark. The salt is dissolving, the debt spreading out into the current, invisible and vast.

I turn to follow. I do not look back at the platform, or the empty space where the timber lay, or the water that is already rising to fill the gap. I am not here to mourn the cargo. I am here to keep the count.

"Mara," I call out, my voice steady over the sound of the rushing water. "I am coming. Keep him awake."

I step forward, the water closing in behind me, and I do not stop.

Mara’s grip is iron against my ribs. I do not fight it. I let the weight of my body hang from her shoulder, a dead thing that has forgotten how to be alive. The water is cold, a living thing that presses against my legs, trying to pull me down into the dark. I keep my eyes open. I force them open.

"Kell," I say. The word is small, scraped from the back of my throat. "Keep the numbers dry. The debt will wait."

I do not look back. I look at the white slit of light ahead, the only thing in this tunnel that is not water or debt. I take a step. My foot finds the wet brick, slick and cold. I take another. The pain is a white spike behind my eyes, sharp and bright, but I do not stop. I am not counting the cost of the muscle I burn. I am only moving.

Mara’s knees buckle at the threshold. The light is no longer a slit but a wall, bright and blinding after the tunnel’s dark. I stop, my boots finding the uneven stone of the shore. The water behind me is a roar, a living thing that wants to swallow the debt and the man and me all at once.

I look down at Dell. His head is still lolling, his eyes half-closed, the white spike of pain still visible in his face. He is awake, but barely. He is choosing to stay in the dark with me rather than open his eyes to the world.

I let him sink to his knees in the wet sand. The salt is in my hair, in my mouth, on my skin. I can feel the cold seeping into my bones, a heavy, slow ache that will last for days. I do not brush it off. I do not wipe the water from my face.

"Kell," I say, my voice raw. "The ledger."

I do not turn around. I am not ready to see his face, not yet. I am not ready to see the debt in his eyes, the weight of the numbers he is carrying against his chest. I am only here to make sure the man is alive, and that the debt is still ours to pay.

I stand up, my legs trembling, and look out at the harbour. The town is there, the lights of the houses, the masts of the ships. It is real. It is solid. The water has not taken it all.

"Dell," I say, reaching out to steady him. "Open your eyes. The debt is not gone. It is just waiting for us."

The salt air hits my face, sharp and stinging, and I stop at the threshold. The roar of the water behind me is a living thing, a hungry mouth that has already swallowed the first crate and the debt it carried. I do not look back at the tunnel. I look at Mara, who is still standing in the wet sand, her hands trembling as she holds Dell upright.

I reach into my coat. My fingers find the ledger, dry and warm against my chest, a small, hard thing in the cold world. I pull it out, holding it up so the light catches the pages. The paper is unmarked. The numbers are safe.

"Mara," I say, my voice steady over the wind. "The debt is still here. It is just waiting for us."

I step forward, the wet sand sinking into my boots, and I hold the ledger out to her. My hands are steady. I am not counting the cost of the muscle I burn, or the time we lose. I am only waiting for her to take it, and for the water to stop rising.

I feel the weight of the book in her hands before I see it. It is dry. It is solid. The debt has a body now, and it is sitting in Mara’s palms. I open my eyes. The light is too bright, too white, and the harbour looks like a painting of itself, stiff and clean.

I look at Kell. He is standing behind her, his coat soaked, his face blank. He is waiting for the numbers to mean something. I look at Mara. She is holding the ledger out, her hands steady, her face a mask of exhaustion.

I take the book from her. The paper is warm, a small, dry thing against my cold skin. I do not open it. I do not need to. I know the numbers. I have carried them since the last winter, when the water took my breath and I held on to the brick just to keep the count.

"The debt is here," I say. My voice is a scrape, a rough thing in the salt air. "We are here. It will wait."

I look at the water, still churning at the tunnel’s mouth, still hungry. I look at the town, the masts, the lights. I am alive. I am wet. I am holding the debt.

I do not move. I wait for Mara to tell me what comes next.

Mara takes the book from his hands. It is lighter than the cargo, lighter than Dell, but it weighs more against my palms. I hold it out, not to Kell, but to the air between us, so we can all see it. The pages are dry. The ink is dark. The debt is real.

I look at Dell. He is standing, barely, his knees still shaking in the wet sand. He is alive. He is here. He is holding the count in his head, and I am holding the proof in my hands.

"The cod is gone," I say. My voice is quiet, but it cuts through the wind. "The first crate is at the bottom of the harbour. The salt is in the water. The debt is in the book."

I turn to face the tunnel. The water is still moving, still hungry, but it is behind us now. It is not coming back for the second or third crate. Those are on the platform, safe and dry, waiting to be counted.

"We did not lose the cargo," I say, turning back to them. "We lost a part of it. The rest is ours. The debt is ours. And we are all here to pay it."

I close my fingers around the ledger, pressing it against my chest, right over my own heart.

"Let's go," I say. "Before the water decides it wants more."

Kell watches the ledger settle into Mara’s chest. The wool of her coat is damp, but the book is dry. I do not reach for it. I do not ask to see the numbers again. The count is not in the paper anymore; it is in the fact that we are standing in the salt air, breathing.

I look at Dell. He is leaning against the dune grass, his face the color of old rope. He is alive. That is a number I can live with.

I turn my back on the tunnel. The water is still churning, a dark mouth trying to close, but it is behind me now. I do not look back.

"Move," I say. "The wind is picking up, and the ledger needs a dry room, not a wet hand."

I start walking toward the town, my boots sinking into the sand. I wait for them to follow. I do not rush. I have kept the count long enough to know that the debt does not care how fast we walk, only that we do not stop.

Dell does not argue. He lets the ledger settle into Mara’s chest, a dry, hard weight against the damp wool. The wind is colder here than it was in the tunnel, carrying the scent of tar and salt that he has not smelled in months. His legs still shake, a tremor that starts in his knees and climbs up into his ribs. He grips the edge of the dune grass, his fingers white against the stalks.

"I am not a number," I say. My voice is thin, scraped raw by the cold. "I am the man who paid for the first crate. I am the one who held the beam."

I look at Kell. He is already walking, his back straight, his eyes on the town lights. He is not looking at me. He is not looking at the water. He is looking at the debt.

"Move," I repeat, though the word is already gone, swallowed by the wind. I push off the grass, my boots sinking into the wet sand. I do not run. I do not stop. I walk toward the town, toward the dry room, toward the end of the count. The water behind me is still churning, but it is no longer a voice. It is just a sound.

I do not turn around. The wind is too strong for it, and my legs are still shaking, a tremor that starts in my knees and climbs up into my ribs. I hear Kell’s boots in the wet sand, steady and sure, and I hear Dell’s breath, thin and scraped raw.

I keep my hand pressed against the ledger. The book is dry, but my coat is not. The salt is drying in my hair, stiffening the strands into a cold, white cage. I do not brush it off. I do not wipe the water from my face.

"Kell," I say, my voice low, meant only for him. "Keep the numbers dry. The debt will wait for us on the other side."

I take a step. My boot sinks into the sand, cold and heavy. I take another. The water behind us is still churning, a dark, hungry thing that wants to swallow the debt and the man and me all at once. I do not look back. I am not counting the cost of the muscle I burn, or the time we lose. I am only moving.

I stop walking. The wind is a physical weight against my chest, pushing me toward the town, but my feet are planted in the wet sand. I do not turn my head. I do not need to see the ledger against Mara’s coat to know it is dry. I can feel the dryness in the air, in the way the salt is crunching under my boots.

"Mara," I say. My voice is not a shout. It is a flat, hard line in the wind. "You are carrying the debt. I am walking beside it."

I take a step. The sand gives way, cold and sucking. I take another. I am not looking at the water. I am not looking at the dark mouth of the tunnel. I am looking at the town, at the lights that are still burning, still real.

"Keep moving," I say. "The numbers do not care if we are tired. They only care if we stop."

I turn to face Kell, then to Dell, who stands in the shadow of the tunnel mouth, his breath a thin white line in the cold.

"The beam was not a choice," I say. "The water was not a choice. I chose to keep the man who holds the count, because the ledger is only paper until a living hand holds it. I chose to let the first crate sink, because the salt is already in the water, and the debt is already in the book."

I pull the rope taut, testing the weight. It holds. It is just rope.

"I did not lose the cargo," I say, my eyes on Kell. "I lost a part of it. The rest is on the platform, dry and waiting. The debt is not gone. It is just waiting for us to pay it. And I will not pay it with a body in the water, because then the count is not clean. It is buried."

I let the rope slip from my fingers, letting it hang loose again.

"Write it down," I tell Kell. "The first crate is gone. The man is here. The debt is ours. That is the number. That is the truth."

I turn back to Dell, my hand moving to his shoulder, steady and warm.

"Move," I say. "The wind is picking up, and the ledger needs a dry room, not a wet hand."

Mara’s hand is on my shoulder, warm and heavy. It is not a question. It is a weight I can hold.

I do not look at the rope. I do not look at the dark mouth of the tunnel. I look at Kell, who is still standing in the light, his face hard and waiting.

"The count is clean," I say. My voice is thin, scraped raw by the cold, but it is steady. "The first crate is gone. The man is here. The debt is ours."

I let the words sit there, heavy and wet, while the wind pulls at my coat. I am not counting the cost of the muscle I burn, or the time we lose. I am only moving.

I take a step. My boot sinks into the wet sand, cold and sucking. I take another. I am not running. I am not stopping. I walk toward the town, toward the dry room, toward the end of the count. The water behind me is still churning, but it is no longer a voice. It is just a sound.

Before Dell’s third step reaches dry sand, the ledger in Mara’s coat snaps open in the wind and a wet page tears free, tumbling into the black mouth of the tunnel. Kell lunges and snatches it by the corner, but the water has already swallowed half the ink, smearing the number into a long blue streak. The tunnel exhales a low, hollow knock from behind the brick.

Mara steps between Kell and the tunnel mouth, her hand closing on the torn page’s edge as the hollow knock repeats from deeper in the brick. The water answers with a sharp crack, splitting the blue streak across the wet page and sending a black stain racing toward the ledger’s number. Kell’s lantern swings toward the dark.

Mara presses the torn page flat against the ledger with both palms, her thumb pinning the split blue streak closed before Kell can read the ruined number. The lantern’s light swings into the hole, and something wet and heavy slides across the brick lip, dragging a thin line of salt into the sand.

The salt line is fresh. It is not a mark. It is a wound.

I watch it drag across the sand, thin and white, cutting the dark wet ground. The knock comes again, low and hollow, from behind the brick. It is not the water. Water does not knock. Water rushes, or swallows, or hisses. This is a hand on the other side of a door.

The salt line is fresh. It is not a mark. It is a wound.

I watch it drag across the sand, thin and white, cutting the dark wet ground. The knock comes again, low and hollow, from behind the brick. It is not the water. Water does not knock. Water rushes, or swallows, or hisses. This is a hand on the other side of a door.

I look at Mara. Her palms are flat on the ledger, pinning the torn page down. She is holding the debt shut. She is holding the number closed. I look at Kell. He is standing in the light, his face hard, his eyes on the rope, on the dark, on the line of salt. He is waiting for me to say it. He is waiting for the count to break.

I step forward. My boot sinks into the sand, cold and sucking. I do not stop. I step again. My ribs ache, a sharp, bright thing under the cold. I am not a number. I am the man who held the beam. I am the one who paid for the first crate.

I stand between them. I stand in the light.

"The count is clean," I say. My voice is thin, scraped raw by the wind, but it is steady. "The first crate is gone. The man is here. The debt is ours."

I let the words sit there, heavy and wet. I do not look at the tunnel. I do not look at the rope. I look at Mara, then at Kell. I am still here. I am still counting.

I take a step toward the town. My legs shake, a tremor that starts in my knees and climbs up into my ribs. I do not run. I do not stop. I walk toward the dry room, toward the end of the count. The water behind me is still churning, but it is no longer a voice. It is just a sound.

trace.title: Kell speaks
trace.detail:
I stand where the salt line ends. The lantern is still in my hand, its flame a thin, white needle against the dark. I have not moved since the page tore. I am here. I am not gone. I am not the rope, and I am not the water.

I look at the torn page in Mara’s hands. The blue streak is a wound in the paper. I look at Dell. He is standing in the light, his face the color of old rope, his eyes fixed on me. He is not moving. He is not speaking. The silence between us is not empty; it is full of the sound of the water behind him, and the salt drying on his skin.

I close the distance. The wet sand gives way under my boots, cold and sucking. I stop a step away from him, close enough to see the tremor in his hands, close enough to see the way his ribs move with each shallow breath. I do not touch him. I do not ask if he is hurt. I have seen the way the beam fell, and I have felt the ledger against my chest, dry and hard, while the water rushed in to fill the space it left behind.

"Dell," I say. My voice is low, matching the wind. "What happened down there?"

I close the distance. The wet sand gives way under my boots, cold and sucking. I stop a step away from her, close enough to see the tremor in her hands, close enough to see the way her ribs move with each shallow breath. I do not touch the book. I do not ask if she is hurt. I have seen the way the page tore, and I have felt the weight of the debt in my own chest, dry and hard, while the water rushed in to fill the space it left behind.

"Mara," I say. My voice is low, matching the wind. "The number is gone. The ink is in the water. The count is not clean yet."

I look at Dell, then at the slack rope, then back at Mara. I am waiting for the number. I am waiting for the lie that will let us keep walking.

"Tell me," I say. "The debt is not gone. It is just waiting for us to pay it."
